lead: A set is an unordered collection of unique items. You cannot index it, but you can ask whether a value is inside, and you can combine two sets with union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference. Sets exist because some questions are about membership and overlap, not order: which students joined both the Python club and the coding contest, which UPI transaction ids appear twice in a log. Python stores a set in a hash table, so a membership test stays fast even when the set holds lakhs of items.
prereq: You need: 3.3 for mutability and 3.5 for why a tuple of numbers is hashable but a list is not.

sections.h3: What a set is, and how to build one

blocks.text: A set holds each value at most once and gives no position to any value. A set literal uses braces: A = {1, 2, 3} makes a set of three integers. Braces alone are ambiguous, because {} is an empty dictionary, so the empty set is written set().
The constructor set(iterable) builds a set from any sequence and drops duplicates silently. set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) gives {1, 2, 3}. set("banana") gives {'b', 'a', 'n'}.

items: There is no indexing and no slicing. A[0] raises TypeError, because a set keeps no order.
Iteration order is not guaranteed. A for loop over a set can visit the items in a different order on a different run, so never depend on it.
Only hashable items fit. Numbers, strings and tuples of hashable items are fine; a list or a dictionary is rejected, because it can change after it is stored.

blocks.text: Deduplication is the everyday use. Collect the UPI transaction ids of one day into a list, pass the list to set(), and len() of the result is the number of distinct payments. Convert back with sorted() when a fixed order is needed.

A.add(x) inserts x; if x is already there, nothing changes and no error is raised. A.remove(x) deletes x and raises KeyError when x is absent. A.discard(x) deletes x and says nothing when x is absent. A.pop() removes and returns an arbitrary item, not the smallest or the first. A.clear() empties the set, and len(A) counts the items.

The in test is the reason sets exist. x in A costs about the same for ten items and for ten lakh items, because Python hashes x, computes a slot and looks there. A list has to compare items one by one; see 3.9.

blocks.code:
payments = ["T1", "T2", "T1", "T3", "T2"]
seen = set()
for txn in payments:
    seen.add(txn)
print(len(payments), len(seen))
print("T2" in seen)
seen.discard("T9")
print(sorted(seen))

sections.h3: Union, intersection, difference and subset tests

blocks.text: Four operators combine two sets. Union A | B holds every item of either set. Intersection A & B holds the items in both. Difference A - B holds the items of A that are not in B. Symmetric difference A ^ B holds the items in exactly one of the two sets.

Each operator has a method form: A.union(B), A.intersection(B), A.difference(B), A.symmetric_difference(B). The methods accept any iterable, so A.union([7, 8]) works. The operators need a set on both sides, so A | [7, 8] raises TypeError.

Comparison operators test whole-set containment. A <= B is True when every item of A lies in B, that is A is a subset of B. A >= B is True when A contains every item of B, that is A is a superset. A < B and A > B are the strict forms and are False when the two sets are equal. A.isdisjoint(B) is True when the sets share no item.

frozenset is the immutable twin: F = frozenset({1, 2}). It has the same read-only methods and the same operators, but no add or remove. Because it never changes, it is hashable, so it can be a dictionary key or an item of another set. Only a few universities ask for it in depth.

examples.question: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. Find A | B, A & B, A - B, B - A, A ^ B, state whether A <= B is True, and convert the list [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] into a set. Say what the size of that last set is.
steps: A | B takes every item of either set: 1, 2, 3, 4 from A and 5 from B, so A | B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, which has 5 items.
A & B keeps only items present in both: 1 is missing from B, 2 is missing from B, 3 and 4 are in both. So A & B = {3, 4}, 2 items.
A - B keeps items of A that are not in B: 1 and 2. So A - B = {1, 2}, 2 items.
B - A keeps items of B that are not in A: only 5. So B - A = {5}, 1 item.
A ^ B keeps items in exactly one set: from A that is 1 and 2, from B that is 5. So A ^ B = {1, 2, 5}, 3 items.
A <= B asks whether every item of A is in B. Check each item: 1 is not in B, so the answer is False. (2 is missing too.)
set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) inserts 3, skips the second 3, inserts 1, inserts 2 and skips the second 1. The set is {1, 2, 3}, so the size is 3.
Turning {1, 2, 3} back with list() gives an order produced by hashing, not the order 3, 1, 2 of the original list; use sorted() for a fixed order.
examples.check:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}
B = {3, 4, 5}
print(sorted(A | B))
print(sorted(A & B))
print(sorted(A - B))
print(sorted(B - A))
print(sorted(A ^ B))
print(int(A <= B))
print(sorted(set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])))

traps: {} is an empty dictionary, not an empty set. The empty set is set(), and the examiner often asks for both in one question.
remove(x) raises KeyError when x is absent, while discard(x) returns silently. pop() on an empty set also raises KeyError.
A set has no order: A[0] and A[1:2] raise TypeError, and the printed order of a set is not the order in which the items were added.
The operators need sets on both sides. A | [7, 8] raises TypeError, while A.union([7, 8]) is accepted.
A <= B means subset, not 'numerically smaller'. A < B is strictly smaller as a set, so it is False when A and B hold the same items.

quiz.q: What does set([4, 4, 5, 4]) contain, and how many items does it have?
quiz.a: {4, 5}, with 2 items. The constructor drops duplicates.

quiz.q: Which expression creates an empty set, and what does {} create instead?
quiz.a: set() creates an empty set. {} creates an empty dictionary.

quiz.q: Why is a list rejected as an item of a set while a tuple of integers is accepted?
quiz.a: Set items must be hashable and their hash must not change while stored. A list is mutable, so it is unhashable. A tuple of integers is immutable and every item is hashable, so the tuple itself is hashable.

quiz.q: Give one difference between A - B and A ^ B.
quiz.a: A - B keeps only items of A that are not in B, so items that lie only in B are dropped. A ^ B keeps items in exactly one set, so it also keeps the items that lie only in B; A ^ B = (A - B) | (B - A).

quiz.q: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}. Give A ^ B, A - B and A.isdisjoint(B).
quiz.a: A ^ B = {1, 2, 4}; A - B = {1, 2}; A.isdisjoint(B) is False because 3 belongs to both sets.

quiz.q: s = {10, 20, 30}. The code runs s.discard(20) and then s.remove(40). What is s, and what happens at the second call?
quiz.a: discard(20) leaves s = {10, 30}. remove(40) finds no 40 and raises KeyError, so s stays {10, 30}.

quiz.q: Two lists of 1,00,000 ids each must be compared for shared ids. Why is a set-based check faster than two nested loops?
quiz.a: Building a set is O(n) on average and each in test is O(1) on average, so the check is about 2n hash lookups, roughly 2,00,000 steps. Nested loops make 1,00,000 x 1,00,000 = 10^10 comparisons.

quiz.q: A program that prints a set of strings gives a different order on two runs. Is the set faulty? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A set stores no order. The position of a string depends on its hash value and the table size, and Python randomises string hashing per run, so the print order can change. Wrap the set in sorted() when a fixed order is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Relational databases run on the same algebra: SQL's UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT are the set operators above, and the query planner weighs them the same way. A search engine keeps an inverted index, which is a dictionary from a word to a set of document ids, and answers a two-word query with an intersection. Data cleaning pipelines keep a set of seen ids so no record is processed twice. When the universe is small integers, a bit array or a NumPy boolean mask is lighter and faster than a Python set. Look up CPython's set implementation and hash randomisation (PYTHONHASHSEED) to see why the order changes between runs.
